title: Short Stuff: The Best Episode Since Sliced Bread
summary: Short Stuff episode on sliced bread. Josh and Chuck trace the idea from bread's ancient origins through Otto Frederick Rohwedder's slicing machine (worked on from 1917, first sold 1928 to baker Frank Bench in Missouri after a shop fire destroyed his prototype and blueprints), Gustav Papendick's improvement with wrapping, early marketing to homemakers, Wonder Bread's name origin, and the 1943 World War II wartime attempt by US Food Administrator Claude R. Wickard to ban sliced bread, which was reversed after public outcry. They close with Rohwedder's later life in Iowa and Louisiana and Bench's sales jump.

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor shout-outs
segments.summary: Josh introduces the short episode, with Jerry sitting in for Dave. Chuck and Josh give thanks to sponsors and introduce the topic of sliced bread, noting bread's long history.

segments.title: Bread's long history and early sandwiches
segments.summary: The hosts note bread is tens of thousands of years old, but sliced bread is under a century old. They describe pre-sliced bread's long absence, mention Hillel the Elder's sandwich and Leslie Eliza Leslie's 1840 ham sandwich directions, and say people sliced bread at home before July 7, 1928.

segments.title: Otto Frederick Rohwedder and the 1917 fire
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce Otto Frederick Rohwedder, the inventor credited as father of sliced bread. He worked on a slicer from 1917, and a fire at his office destroyed his prototype and blueprints. Chuck notes he was a jeweler with an ophthalmology degree who sold jewelry stores to fund the idea.

segments.title: First slicer, hatpin fix, and Papendick's wrapping
segments.summary: Rohwedder's first working machine was foot-pumped and produced half-inch slices that fell apart. The first machine was sold to Frank Bench, a Missouri baker at the Chillicothe Baking Company, and the second to Gustav Papendick, who improved it with wrapping. Before that, Rohwedder's fix was a hatpin through the loaf.

segments.title: Marketing sliced bread to homemakers and Wonder Bread
segments.summary: The first print reference to sliced bread was a 1928 Missouri newspaper ad saying 'Sliced bread is made here.' Homemakers were the early adopters who saw time savings. Wonder Bread, originally called Wonder Cut, became a widely available sliced brand.

segments.title: Wartime attempt to ban sliced bread
segments.summary: During World War II, US Food Administrator Claude R. Wickard ordered a ban on sliced bread as part of wartime conservation. The stated reasons were wax paper and paraffin use and grain prices. Homemakers protested strongly and Wickard backed down.

segments.title: Rohwedder's later life and Frank Bench's success
segments.summary: Rohwedder sold his patent to the Micro-Westco Company in Iowa and worked as a salesperson for its bakery machine division. He retired in 1971, lived quietly in Louisiana, and died near age eighty. Bench's sales rose about 2,000 percent after he began selling sliced bread. The hosts joke about name pronunciation and Clark's origin.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the short episode.
